questions.q: In the worked lab example, the control group measured 620/1000 ideal outcomes and the treatment group measured 710/1000. What did the computed z-score (~4.26) indicate?
options: Readout mitigation works on every circuit and device, universally
The 0.09 difference is extremely unlikely to be explained by shot noise alone
The experiment was run incorrectly and must be discarded
The two groups actually measured the same probability
questions.explain: A z-score of about 4.26 is far beyond the common 1.96 threshold for 95% confidence, meaning the observed 0.09 difference is extremely unlikely to have arisen from random shot noise alone -- it does not, however, license the universal claim in option C.

questions.q: Why does the lesson caution against concluding, from this one lab result, that readout mitigation improves results on all circuits and devices?
options: The result is specific to one circuit, one device, and one calibration window -- the honest, bounded claim this course has emphasized throughout
Because 1,000 shots is considered too few to draw any conclusion at all
Because readout mitigation never works on any other circuit
Because the z-test calculation was actually wrong
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states the conclusion applies to 'this specific circuit, this specific device, this specific calibration window' -- generalizing beyond that would overstate what was actually shown, echoing the overstatement red flags from the paper-reading lesson.

questions.q: What is the key difference between 'statistical significance' and 'effect size,' per this lesson?
options: Significance measures how unlikely a difference is due to random noise; effect size measures how large or important the difference actually is -- a result can have one without the other
They are two names for the exact same calculation
Effect size is only relevant for simulators, not hardware
Significance measures how large a difference is, while effect size measures randomness
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates the two: a large shot count can make a tiny difference statistically significant without it being practically important, and a real effect can fail to reach significance with too few shots -- both numbers are needed for the full picture.

questions.q: Why did the lab's experimental design call for interleaving control and treatment runs across the queue window, rather than running all of one condition first?
options: To average out hardware drift across both groups, consistent with the controls lesson's design principles
Because IBM Quantum hardware requires alternating job submission by policy
Because interleaving produces more shots per run
Because interleaving removes the need for a z-test
questions.explain: This directly reuses the Lesson 4 principle: interleaving runs over time prevents hardware drift from confounding one group more than the other.

questions.q: If an experiment instead measured a much smaller difference (0.615 vs. 0.635) at the same 1,000 shots per condition, what would you expect about its statistical significance, based on how effect size and shot count both feed into the z-score?
options: It would be impossible to compute a z-score for a smaller difference
It would likely fall below the significance threshold, since a much smaller observed difference produces a smaller z-score at the same shot count
Significance is completely unrelated to the size of the observed difference
It would be automatically more significant, since smaller differences are always more significant
questions.explain: The z-score scales with the size of the observed difference (holding shot count fixed), so a much smaller observed difference produces a much smaller z-score, making it less likely to cross the significance threshold -- as a direct calculation confirms (z drops to about 0.92, below 1.96).
